abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) genes form a large and functionally diverse superfamily of heme-thiolate monooxygenases that catalyse the oxidation of endogenous and exogenous compounds. Within this superfamily, CYP4 enzymes primarily act on fatty acids, substrates central to energy metabolism. Sustained flight and long distance migration in birds rely on efficient fatty acid use, making CYP4 a pertinent system for examining how lipid associated functions may vary across avian lineages. Here, we characterised the evolution of CYP4 genes across 363 avian whole genomes, representing over 90% of bird families, to investigate patterns of molecular evolution and their association with ecological and life history variation. We identified four CYP4 subfamilies and analysed sequence evolution using site-models, branch-models, and branch-site models. Our analyses revealed conserved elements of the avian CYP4 repertoire alongside lineage-specific heterogeneity in selective constraint. Several amino acid sites under positive selection were located within substrate recognition sites, regions influencing substrate binding and catalysis. Branch-model analyses identified trait-associated variation in selective pressure across feeding habits, migration and primary lifestyle, with gene-specific patterns. Migration-associated differences in ω remained below one, indicating variation in the strength of selective constraint among migration categories. Branch-site analyses revealed evidence of episodic positive selection associated with migratory lineages. Overall, these results highlight site-specific adaptive evolution within CYP4 genes alongside broader variation in selective constraint, providing insight into the evolution of lipid associated metabolic pathways during avian diversification.
